facts.claim: "I Lied" is a duet between Lord Huron and August Ponthier. Ponthier is credited as featured vocalist on the track, which appears on the 2021 album Long Lost.
All tracks on Long Lost, including "I Lied", were written by Ben Schneider. Schneider is also the album's producer.

Discogs credits for Long Lost list Ben Schneider as writer and producer, with Ben Tolliday and Mark Barry as co-producers. Tolliday, Barry and Willem Bleeker are listed as engineers, the album was recorded at Whispering Pines Studios, and it was mastered at Sterling Sound.
Long Lost was recorded at Lord Huron's own Los Angeles studio, Whispering Pines.
For Long Lost, Schneider and bandmates Mark Barry, Miguel Briseño and Tom Renaud recorded live together in the studio for the first time.
Schneider cited classic country duets, such as Conway Twitty and Loretta Lynn and George Jones and Tammy Wynette, as an influence on "I Lied".
Atwood Magazine described "I Lied" as a poetic heartbreak duet.

Ponthier has said she recorded a demo vocal in about an hour in her bedroom after being connected through a mutual contact. She has also said the day she recorded the final vocal at Schneider's 1970s-style studio was the day they met.

Long Lost was written as if the songs came from fictional characters connected to the Whispering Pines studio. In this concept "I Lied" is credited to a fictional duo, Donny & Midge, and the music video presents it as an on-air recording session at Whispering Pines.
Lord Huron is a Los Angeles-based band that Ben Schneider founded in 2010 as a solo project. The name comes from Lake Huron, which Schneider grew up visiting.

research.lineage: The song draws on 1960s–70s country male–female duets (Conway Twitty/Loretta Lynn, George Jones/Tammy Wynette) within Lord Huron's cinematic, retro-flavoured Americana-tinged indie folk rock.

draft:
Every verse of **"I Lied"** is built like a trap. A line opens on a promise, "I swore that I'd become a better man for you, and I tried," and then lets it ride for a beat before the floor drops out on the last three words. Ben Schneider wrote it so the vows come first and the confession arrives late, the way a guilty person tells the truth: after the speech, almost under the breath.

What makes it sting is that the lies aren't the cruel kind. They're the vows people make in love: forever, no one else, I'll never leave. The narrator meant them, or wanted to. By the third verse the song turns stranger: "I read your letter in the morning by the lake, and I cried," and then, "They were tears of joy, my chains are finally broken." That's the feeling at the center, and it's an ugly one to admit. Relief and guilt sit in the same body. Freedom arrives on the back of someone else's goodbye, and the song never apologizes for the joy or pretends it doesn't hurt. Then the confession repeats, six times over, until "Ooh, I lied" stops sounding like an admission and starts sounding like a hymn.

Schneider has cited Conway Twitty and Loretta Lynn and George Jones and Tammy Wynette as models, and you can hear the old country duet's taste for heartbreak played straight. The bend is in how the two voices meet. August Ponthier's harmony sits higher, and the two voices sing the confession together, so the duet doesn't feel like a quarrel between two people. It sounds like two people agreeing on the worst thing about themselves. Both voices are breathy, held long, close to a sigh.

The arrangement stays out of the way. Fingerpicked acoustic guitar rolls through arpeggios, the bass holds long low notes under each chord, a light beat keeps time, and sustained chords hang high in the background. The tempo is slow and swaying, a last-dance tempo, and the production is clean enough that you can hear the room around the players. On *Long Lost* the band recorded live together in their Los Angeles studio, Whispering Pines, for the first time. The album's conceit credits this song to a fictional duo, Donny & Midge, and its video stages it as an on-air session there.

There's a quiet irony in the making of it. Ponthier cut a demo in her bedroom in about an hour, then recorded the final vocal on the day she and Schneider first met. Two near-strangers made a song about how little a lifetime of promises can mean, and they made it sound like years of history.

The song lets you feel the shameful lightness of being let go, so each "I lied" lands as a wound and a release at once.
